content: 1. The study by Mauer AM in 1991 explored whether interventions should be implemented to modify serum lipid levels in children. This research, published in the Annual Review of Nutrition, examined the potential benefits and risks of such interventions. 2. Te Morenga and Montez conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2017 to evaluate the health effects of saturated and trans-fatty acid intake in children and adolescents. Their findings, published in PLoS One, highlighted the impact of these fats on health outcomes in younger populations. 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued guidelines on saturated fatty acid (SFA) and trans-fatty acid (TFA) intake for both adults and children. These guidelines emphasize limiting total fat intake from industrially produced and ruminant TFAs to reduce health risks. 4. The DISC Collaborative Research Group investigated the efficacy and safety of reducing dietary fat and cholesterol intake in children with elevated low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol. Their findings, published in JAMA in 1995, demonstrated the potential benefits of dietary interventions in managing cholesterol levels in children. 5. A prospective randomized trial conducted by Lapinleimu et al. in 1995 involved 1,062 infants and assessed the effects of a diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol. Published in The Lancet, the study provided evidence on the long-term health implications of early dietary modifications. 6. The STRIP study, led by Pahkala et al. in 2020, examined the effects of 20 years of infancy-onset dietary counseling on cardiometabolic risk factors. Published in The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health, the study included a six-year post-intervention follow-up, demonstrating the sustained benefits of early dietary interventions. 7. Xiang and Kingwell, in their 2019 publication in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, discussed the evolving understanding of high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol. They provided a clinician's guide to rethinking the role of good cholesterol in cardiovascular health. 8. Bertram et al. in 2018 estimated the return on investment for prevention and treatment services targeting non-communicable diseases. Published in The Lancet, their analysis highlighted the economic and health benefits of investing in such interventions. 9. Downs et al. conducted a systematic review in 2018 to assess the impact of policies aimed at reducing trans-fat consumption. Published in Current Developments in Nutrition, the study evaluated evidence on the effectiveness of these policies in improving public health outcomes. 10. Marklund et al. in 2020 modeled the health benefits, costs, and cost-effectiveness of eliminating industrial trans-fatty acids in Australia. Their findings, published in PLoS Medicine, demonstrated the potential for significant health improvements and economic savings. 11. Dall et al. in 2009 analyzed the potential health benefits and medical cost savings from reducing calorie, sodium, and saturated fat intake in the American diet. Published in the American Journal of Health Promotion, their study emphasized the importance of dietary changes for public health. 12. Meier et al. in 2015 conducted a health econometric analysis to estimate healthcare costs associated with adequate intake of sugars, salt, and saturated fat in Germany. Published in PLoS One, the study provided insights into the economic burden of poor dietary habits. 13. Malla et al. in 2005 estimated healthcare savings from the use of trans-fat-free canola oil in Canada. Published in Acta Agriculturae Scandinavica, their study highlighted the economic and health benefits of replacing trans fats with healthier alternatives. 14. Abdullah et al. in 2017 evaluated the health benefits and healthcare cost savings of substituting oils rich in monounsaturated fatty acids for conventional dietary oils in the United States. Published in Nutrition Reviews, their findings supported the use of healthier oils to improve public health outcomes. 15. Schultz et al. in 2018 examined the relationship between socioeconomic status and cardiovascular outcomes. Published in Circulation, their study identified challenges and potential interventions to address health disparities. 16. Allen et al. in 2017 conducted a systematic review to explore the relationship between socioeconomic status and non-communicable disease risk factors in lowand lower-middle-income countries. Published in The Lancet Global Health, their findings emphasized the need for targeted interventions in these populations. 17. Teicholz, in her 2014 book The Big Fat Surprise, argued for the inclusion of butter, meat, and cheese in a healthy diet. Her work challenged conventional dietary guidelines and sparked debate on the role of saturated fats in health. 18. Malhotra in 2013 published an article in BMJ asserting that saturated fat is not the primary issue in cardiovascular health. His work called for a reevaluation of dietary recommendations regarding fat intake. 19. Jousilahti et al. in 2016 conducted a population-based observational study in Eastern Finland, examining the impact of primary prevention and risk factor reduction on coronary heart disease mortality over 40 years. Published in BMJ, their findings highlighted the effectiveness of public health interventions. 20. Vartiainen et al. in 2016 analyzed changes in serum cholesterol and diet in North Karelia and Finland. Published in Global Heart, their study demonstrated the success of dietary interventions in reducing cholesterol levels and improving public health. 21. Smed et al. in 2016 evaluated the effects of Denmark's saturated fat tax on food and nutrient intake and modeled health outcomes. Published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition, their study provided evidence on the effectiveness of fiscal policies in promoting healthier diets. 22. The WHO's 2022 report on global trans-fat elimination outlined progress and challenges in reducing trans-fat consumption worldwide. The report emphasized the importance of adhering to updated guidelines to improve public health outcomes. 23. The WHO's updated recommendations on saturated and trans-fatty acid intake aim to limit total TFA intake to 1% or less of total energy intake. These guidelines align with recommendations to limit SFA intake to less than 10% of total energy, with potential implications for dairy consumption. 24. The modeling exercise conducted by Emeritus Professor C. Murray Skeaff examined the impact of updated WHO recommendations on dairy consumption. The study highlighted the importance of balancing TFA and SFA intake while maintaining adequate dairy consumption. 25. The analysis included data on the TFA and SFA composition of milk, cheese, and butter, emphasizing the need for consistency in dietary recommendations across different populations and regions.
